title: Vasquez on Ps 142: even after justification, venials remain
source_text: XXXIV. Testis sit Vasquez ipse inter Pontificios rigidissimus justitiae inhaerentis assertor, is enim Tom. 2. in primam secundae disput. 222. cap. 6. num. 44. ad locum sibi objectum ex Psalmo 142. juxta versionem vulgatam, respondet. Psalmista me-rito a Deo postulat ne intret cum ipso in judicium, hoc est, ne ipsum judicet non prae-via misericordia gratiae suae. Nam, inquit, nisi prius Deus misericordia sua ipsum praeveniat, ut a peccatis justificetur, non poterit non in judicio Dei damnari; hoc autem quisque nostrum dicere potest, etiam post justificationem a mortali, quia adhuc multa venialia manent, quae, nisi Dei misericordia deleantur, priusquam ad judicium Dei vocentur, non poterit homo absoluto justificari, hoc est, omnino sine Dei judicio & damnatione liberari.
pass_a_gloss: Let Vasquez himself be witness, among the Papists the most rigid assertor of inherent righteousness: for he, in volume 2 on the Prima Secundae, disputation 222, chapter 6, number 44, answering a place objected to him from Psalm 142 according to the Vulgate version, replies that the Psalmist rightly demands of God that he not enter into judgment with him—that is, that he not judge him without the prior mercy of his grace. For, he says, unless God first prevents him by his mercy so that he is justified from sins, he cannot but be damned in God's judgment; and this each of us can say even after justification from mortal sin, because many venials still remain which, unless they are blotted out by God's mercy before they are called to God's judgment, a man cannot be justified absolutely—that is, altogether freed without God's judgment and damnation.
pass_b_english: Vasquez on Ps 142/143: the Psalmist rightly asks not to be judged without prior mercy.
Even after mortal-sin justification, uncleared venials would damn without mercy.

choices.why: Key lemma for De Justitia densify §1068.
